getting-started.title: 🚀 Getting started
getting-started.text: 🚀 Getting started The folders it needs The plugin is developed next to the projects it uses: go.mod replaces Go Simulator and Go Renderer with the folders beside this one. Clone them side by side: go-renderer/ go-simulator/ go-simulator-urban/ ← this repository GEOS The plugin cuts plots, walls and squares with GEOS, the geometry engine shapely uses. Install it before building: brew install geos # macOS sudo apt install libgeos-dev # Debian, Ubuntu sudo dnf install geos-devel # Fedora pkg-config geos should then print its version. While it is not installed, a .geos-local/env.sh (ignored by git) can point cgo at an unpacked copy: . .geos-local/env.sh before building. A whole rules file The city rule sets up a city and opens every year; its instance name names the city, and the other rules find it by their city parameter, so several cities can grow in one simulation. This is the made-up river town drawn in these pages: plugins: - name: urban command: [go, run, .] directory: ../go-simulator-urban # where the plugin runs stages: - name: city clock: {unit: year, from: -1, to: 100, step: 1} rules: - rule: city name: river_town with: relief: {path: relief.npy, minimum_x: -1.6, minimum_z: -1.6, cell_size: 0.0125} features: inputs.geojson seed: 7 nucleus: [0, -0.12] population: {model: logistic, from_year: 0, from: 600, to_year: 100, to: 36000, ceiling: 42000} open_streets_below: 0.5 centres: [{at: [0, -0.12], weight: 1}, {at: [0.15, 0.35], weight: 0.6, grows_from: 30, grows_for: 30}] max_floors: [{before: 40, floors: 2}, {before: 80, floors: 3}, {floors: 4}] first_wall: {population: 4000} river: {reach: 0.25} squares: {per_inhabitants: 2500} - {rule: densify, with: {city: river_town}} - {rule: expand, with: {city: river_town}} - {rule: walls, with: {city: river_town}} - {rule: prune_empty_streets, with: {city: river_town}, every: 5} - {rule: split_large_blocks, with: {city: river_town}, every: 5} - {rule: space_syntax, with: {city: river_town, samples: 200}, every: 5} - {rule: squares, with: {city: river_town}, every: 5} - {rule: indicators, with: {city: river_town}} inputs.geojson holds the window the town may grow in (a 3 × 3 km square), a river 35 m wide, three roads that meet near the river and an obstacle where nothing is built: Role Geometry window the square from [-1.5, -1.5] to [1.5, 1.5] river ( width: 0.035 ) from [-1.6, 0.25] through [-0.6, 0.12] , [-0.1, 0.05] , [0.4, 0.12] , [1, 0] to [1.6, 0.05] road from [-1.6, -0.35] through [-0.6, -0.2] , [0, -0.12] , [0.7, -0.25] to [1.6, -0.15] road from [0.1, -1.6] through [0.05, -0.6] , [0, -0.12] , [0.05, 0.4] to [0.25, 1.6] road from [0, -0.12] through [-0.5, 0.6] to [-1.2, 1.6] obstacles the quadrilateral [0.8, 0.6] , [1.3, 0.55] , [1.4, 1] , [0.9, 1.1] relief.npy is a grid of heights in metres: a gentle plain, a little lower along the river, with a low hill to the north-west. Without a relief , the city reads the world's elevation field, so the terrain plugin can go first instead. Every key is in the scenario . Running it Without a window, to the end of the clock, saving what the stages ask for: cd ../go-simulator go run ./cmd/simulate -rules <rules.yaml> -output results/ With Go Simulator's viewer, over a glTF scene of the ground, which the town is drawn on as it grows: go run ./cmd/simulator -rules <rules.yaml> scene.glb Go Simulator's running guide has the rest: snapshots, objectives and the viewer's keys. The tests go vet ./... go test ./... Testing has the six synthetic places the tests grow, and how to draw them.

how-it-works.title: 🔍 How it works

sections.text: How the plugin fits Go Simulator

how-it-works.text: 🔍 How it works How the plugin fits Go Simulator Go Simulator is the host. It reads the rules file, keeps the world (its entities, fields and events) and moves the clock. The urban plugin is a separate program the host starts; they talk over standard input and output (Go Simulator's protocol ). main.go only serves the plugin; everything else is in the urban package. At the start the plugin describes itself: its nine rules, their parameters, what each one reads and what it writes. That description is also where the rules reference comes from. The city rule reads the world's elevation field when the scenario gives no relief file. The other rules read nothing from other plugins: they work on the city the city rule set up. The rules write the city's entities ( street , parcel , building , wall , old_wall , square , bridge , river ) and the indicators event; see outputs . A plugin never touches the renderer: it reads its copy of the world and answers with changes (Go Simulator's writing plugins ). Shapes are in world units on the ground plane (x, z, in kilometres) and fields in physical units, as Go Simulator's vocabulary lists. What travels each year The town's rules belong on a stepped clock in years. Every step the host gives each rule of the stage the year, in the order of the rules file; a rule with every: N runs only when N years have passed since its last run. The rules change the city the plugin keeps in memory, and after the host's request the plugin publishes the city once: only the entities that changed since the last time travel back (a new plot, a house with one more floor, a street that became a main street, a new wall). Thousands of plots stay cheap that way, and each kind travels as one batch to draw. The same scenario and seed grow the same town: a test grows a place twice and compares the two ( testing ). How the pictures were made The pictures of the river town (the town at the top of the README, the four years, the chart, the walls, the streets, the floors and the river) were drawn from the plugin's own answers. A small throwaway program, kept outside the repository, ran the real plugin inside a Go Simulator host with the rules file in getting started , stepped it year by year to year 100, kept every year's indicators event and, every five years, the city's entities, and drew them from above. They are SVG drawings with their own light and dark colours, not screenshots of the viewer: the look of a town in 3D comes from the scene and its style, not from this plugin. The six test places in testing were drawn with the repository's own tools/view_snapshot.py , from what the places test saves with URBAN_PLACES_OUTPUT . The diagrams (how it fits, a year, a plot over the years) were drawn by hand in the same style. The two pictures of the example island at the top of the model were in the repository before these pages, and show a different made-up town.

overview.title: Welcome to Go Urban Simulator 👋

sections.text: All the pages, in reading order

overview.text: Welcome to Go Urban Simulator 👋 The urban plugin grows towns , year after year: a village where roads meet becomes a town with streets of its own, squares, bridges and walls. You give it a place (the area it may use, the roads and rivers already there) and how many people live there each year; it finds room for them plot by plot where people would most want to live, and builds streets, squares and walls as the town needs them. Is it for me? ✅ You use Go Simulator and want towns that grow . ✅ You want to set it up by writing a rules file : no programming needed. ✅ You are curious about the science behind it: the pages explain the model with pictures. Where to start Pick the line that sounds like you. If you… Read Time are new and want to see it work 🏴‍☠️ The quest : a market town that grows for a century, in 5 levels 45 min want to run its example Getting started 10 min want to set up a town of your own Writing a scenario 15 min are looking up a parameter Rules reference — All the pages, in reading order The menu on the left (or the files in docs/ ) follows this order. Start Overview : this page The quest Getting started Understand Writing a scenario The model What it writes How it works Testing Reference Rules reference 🚧 Not done yet Pictures of the 3D viewer itself. The pictures in these pages are 2D drawings of what the plugin answered, not screenshots (see how the pictures were made ). Gates in the pictures. The plugin publishes the standing wall's gates as gate points (see outputs ), but the pictures were drawn before, so they do not show them. Grid zones, districts and walls tied to rock are described in the model and the scenario , but the example town in the pictures uses none of them. Words you will meet Word What it means Terminal The window where you type commands: Terminal on macOS and Linux, PowerShell on Windows. Repository A project's folder of files, kept on GitHub. git clone <address> copies it to your computer. Plugin A small program that adds one ability to another: here, one kind of simulation each. Rules file A text file (YAML) that says which plugins to use, with which numbers, for how long: no programming needed. Field A grid of numbers laid over the world: the height of every spot, its temperature, its rain. Quest The tutorial of these docs: short levels, each ending with something that works and an achievement. The family Go Urban Simulator is one of a family of small projects that work together: Project What it does Go Renderer draws 3D scenes and flat interfaces Go UI buttons, panels and whole applications Go UI for Android Android apps that look like Android's own Go Sound sound and music Go Scene Builder 3D scenes from a flat map Go Simulator simulations that change a scene Go Terrain Simulator ground shaped by rivers Go Climate Simulator weather and biomes Go Flora Simulator forests that grow Go Urban Simulator (this one) towns that grow Go Motion Simulator a scene that moves Go for 3DS Go on the Nintendo 3DS ⚠️ All of them are educational experiments , written with an AI assistant and pending review by their author: good for learning and playing, not for production.

rules-reference.title: 📋 Rules of the urban plugin
rules-reference.text: 📋 Rules of the urban plugin Version 0.1.0, protocol 2. Pre-industrial urban growth, year by year, on real relief (Weber et al. 2009; Conzen 1960; Hillier and Iida 2005). This reference is generated from what the plugin itself tells the host (the describe message), so it always matches the code. Parameters go under with: in a rules file; see Go Simulator's rules file reference . Rule What it does city Sets up a city from its scenario (relief, inputs, population curve, centres, grid, floors, walls) and starts each year. Its instance name names the city. densify Fills existing plots before the city spreads (burgage cycle). expand Lays plots along free frontages and opens new streets when none are left. walls Raises the first wall and new ones when the suburbs grow too big. prune_empty_streets Removes dead ends nobody built on after some years. split_large_blocks Cuts an alley across blocks wider than a size (Siksna 1997). space_syntax Angular segment analysis: main streets, the market square and shops. indicators Emits an "indicators" event with the city's form measures in the listed years (every step when none). squares Opens irregular squares at busy crossings, inside gates and at bridgeheads (scenario "squares"). city Sets up a city from its scenario (relief, inputs, population curve, centres, grid, floors, walls) and starts each year. testing.title: 🧪 Testing
testing.text: 🧪 Testing Different kinds of places The plugin is tested on six synthetic places that grow into very different towns, and on every one it checks what must hold anywhere: nothing built in water or on obstacles, no plots on top of each other, nothing outside the window, the floor space the people need and a settled area close to what towns of that size covered. Place Settings Result Coastal village (1,200) sea as obstacle, open_streets_below: 0.3 a ribbon along the shore River market town (6,000) river, wall at 3,000, 0.7 compact core with back streets, across the bridge Hilltop town (2,500) hill 140 m high, square houses rings along the contour lines Planned grid town (8,000) grid zone from the start, 0.7 regular blocks of about 80 m Valley street village (1,500) steep valley sides, river a street village between the slopes Large plain city (80,000) three roads, two centres, 0.5 dense core, two walls, ring road and belt, suburbs URBAN_PLACES_OUTPUT=places go test -run DifferentKinds -v ./urban # -short skips the large city uv run --no-project --with matplotlib python tools/view_snapshot.py places.png places/*/ The picture is what those two commands draw (the window dashed, roads in yellow, rivers blue, obstacles grey, houses by use, walls black), made smaller for this page. Everything else go test ./... URBAN_RULES=path/to/rules.yaml URBAN_UNTIL=20 go test -run RulesFile -cpuprofile cpu.out ./urban The second command runs a rules file inside the test process until a year, with a CPU profile for go tool pprof . Other tests cover the street network, frontages, densification, walls rising in phases or by the calendar, colours from the scenario, and a town grown on the world's elevation field matching the same town grown on the relief file, entity by entity.

the-model.title: 🏘️ The urban growth model

sections.text: Plots fill up, then the town spreads

the-model.text: 🏘️ The urban growth model Old towns grew in a recognisable way. People arrived; first they built along the roads; the houses filled their plots, back and then up; when there was no room left, new streets opened; busy crossings became squares; and one day the town was big and rich enough to build a wall. The urban plugin follows that story year by year, with rules taken from studies of real historic towns. A town on the example island at years 10, 40, 70 and 100: houses along the roads first, then a denser core inside its walls Inhabitants and settled ground of the example town over 100 years, with the year of its first wall The example town: from 300 to 6,000 people in 100 years. It follows the roads and the river, and raises its first wall at year 60. Every rule comes from a published model; the only rule of its own is the walls', because no published model simulates them. It knows nothing about any particular city: the scenario says where, how many people and when. The other pictures in this page show a second made-up town, a river town that grows from 600 to 36,000 people in 100 years; its whole rules file is in getting started . The year Each year, the town asks itself one question: do the people fit? The city rule sets up a city at the start and opens every year. Its instance name names the city; the other rules find it by their city parameter, so several cities can grow in one simulation. Rules run in the order of the rules file, usually: Demand. The population follows its curve ( logistic : from from people in from_year to to in to_year , towards a ceiling ). The floor space the people need is inhabitants × square_metres_per_person ; the deficit is what is missing. Densify (Conzen 1960; Caniggia and Maffei). Before the city spreads, its plots fill up: each year up to a quarter of the plots advance, the most wanted first. The house first takes the back of the plot (coverage up to 0.7, or the house depth the scenario gives) and then gains a floor, up to the year's maximum (new houses start with one floor, or two when the year allows three or more, and never more than the outskirts allow). rare_floors is a quota: at most its share of the plots may stand that high. Plots already that high keep their place in it and the most wanted of the rest fill what is left, so the share does not creep up as the town's most wanted places move. In a dense core, a full plot builds at the back, round a yard. Expand (Weber et al. 2009). What is still missing goes to new plots along the most wanted free frontages: close to the growth centres, on gentle ground (no plot steeper than 0.4), inside the window, out of obstacles and water. A frontage less wanted than open_streets_below waits: a street nearby opens first. When no frontage is left, new streets grow from the network, along a tensor field (Chen et al. 2008) that follows the contours, the roads and the river; organic streets wander, continue from their ends and close into blocks. Walls (the plugin's own rule). The first wall goes up when the population reaches first_wall.population or, at the latest, in first_wall.year . It follows the concave hull of what is built (or the given wall_outline ), tied to the supporting rock when there is one, with gates where roads and main streets cross it (published as gate points) and a clear strip inside. When the suburbs outside hold more than new_wall_when_outside of the floor space and the wall is at least 12 years old, a new one goes up and the old one becomes a ring road with a belt of gardens and convents (Whitehand 1967). Its height can rise over the years ( wall_rise ) or follow the calendar ( wall_heights ). Prune empty streets. Dead ends nobody built on for grace_years go away. Split large blocks (Siksna 1997). An alley crosses blocks wider than maximum_side . Space syntax (Hillier and Iida 2005). Angular segment analysis over the street network, on samples origins within local_radius : the most chosen streets become main streets, the most central square the market, and plots on them shops. Squares. Irregular squares open at busy crossings, inside gates and at bridgeheads, one for every per_inhabitants people, at least spacing apart. Indicators. In the listed years, an indicators event with the measures of the city's form. After every request the plugin publishes the city once ( AfterStep ): only the entities that changed since the last time travel to the host. Plots fill up, then the town spreads A plot is a burgage: a narrow front on a street and a long depth behind it. Densify works on the plots that are already there (steps above); expand lays new ones along free frontages, and only opens streets when the frontages left are not wanted enough. With open_streets_below: 0.3 a town stays a street village along its roads; with 0.5 to 0.7 it opens back streets sooner and grows compact. In the river town (0.5) the first decades are ribbons along the roads and the quays; the back streets come later, when the frontages near the centre run out. Walls and the ring road The river town reaches 4,000 people, its first_wall.population , in year 33, and the wall goes up round what is built. By year 49 too much of the floor space lies outside, so a new wall goes up and the old line becomes a ring road; new plots in a belt along it are large gardens and convents (use extensive ), and the town fills the room between the two walls. Where the city grows Relief : the world's elevation field (put the terrain plugin first), or a relief file. Slopes steer streets along the contours and keep plots off steep ground. When the ground comes from the world and changes (the terrain's erosion rule moves it), the city takes it again at the start of the next year. Growth centres pull the city; a centre can start pulling in a year and grow in weight over some years, so a city gains districts as it grows. The growth radius widens with the population (the settled area goes as N^0.714, its radius as N^0.357). Grid zones lay planned streets on a lattice from a year on. Density falls from the core to the outskirts: narrow fronts, deep houses and more floors in the core; wide plots with gardens and lower houses outside. Districts can set their own density. Streets Every street piece has a class (see outputs ). Roads come with the inputs; quays line the river; a ring follows a wall that was replaced; alleys split large blocks; the rest are streets the town opened. Space syntax turns the most chosen streets and alleys into main streets. In the river town, the three roads carry most of the movement, so only two pieces of the streets it opened become main streets. Rivers Rivers come as river features: a line along the axis with a width (km); their water is an obstacle. With the scenario's river settings they shape the town: streets align with the banks, quays line both banks once the town reaches them, plots by the water are wanted and some become workshops (mills, tanners), and bridges are spaced and square to the river. The river is published as a river entity and quays as streets of class quay . With river: {from_world: true} the town also takes the rivers the world already has, such as the ones the terrain's erosion rule finds where the water gathers, so the town and the ground agree on where the water runs. They are taken once, when the city starts: a town does not move its quays and bridges after a river. Only the parts near the window count, and narrowest (km) leaves out the streams too narrow to shape a town. Clearing the drawn scene When the drawn scene already has something where the city grows (an old town, a forest), a clear feature marks it: at the start the plugin sends a clear_area for the scenario's clear_nodes (holes in the feature are spared), and every year it clears the tree_nodes under the new plots. References Barthelemy, M. and Flammini, A. (2008). Modeling urban street patterns. Caniggia, G. and Maffei, G. L. (1979). Composizione architettonica e tipologia edilizia. Cesaretti, R. et al. (2016). Population-area relationship for medieval European cities. Chen, G. et al. (2008). Interactive procedural street modeling. Conzen, M. R. G. (1960). Alnwick, Northumberland: a study in town-plan analysis. Crucitti, P., Latora, V. and Porta, S. (2006). Centrality measures in spatial networks of urban streets. Hillier, B. and Iida, S. (2005). Network and psychological effects in urban movement. Siksna, A. (1997). The effects of block size and form in North American and Australian city centres. Weber, B. et al. (2009). Interactive geometric simulation of 4D cities. Whitehand, J. W. R. (1967). Fringe belts: a neglected aspect of urban geography. Requirements GEOS, the geometry engine shapely uses: sudo apt install libgeos-dev , sudo dnf install geos-devel or brew install geos . While it is not installed, a .geos-local/env.sh (ignored by git) can point cgo at an unpacked copy: . .geos-local/env.sh before building. More in getting started .

the-quest.title: The urban quest
the-quest.text: The urban quest Grow a market town on a river for a hundred years, one level at a time. Each level teaches one piece of the urban plugin and ends with the town in 3D. The quest map: a road from START through 5 levels — Founder, Builder, Planner, Bridge master and Mason — to a final challenge, Mayor On a gentle plain crossed by a river and two old roads, a village of 300 people is founded where the roads meet. It grows along them, opens streets of its own, takes to its river with quays, bridges and squares, and builds a wall it later outgrows, until six thousand people live in it. Every level has the same shape: the idea (explained with something from everyday life), the rules , a checkpoint to know it works, and an optional bonus . Before you start You need Go 1.25 and GEOS ( sudo apt install libgeos-dev , brew install geos ): the plugin cuts plots and walls with it. Clone the projects side by side and make a folder for the quest: git clone https://github.com/akrck02/go-renderer git clone https://github.com/akrck02/go-scene-builder git clone https://github.com/akrck02/go-simulator git clone https://github.com/akrck02/go-simulator-terrain git clone https://github.com/akrck02/go-simulator-urban mkdir town && cd town go mod init example.com/town The plain plain/main.go writes the ground (4 × 4 km, a river valley, a hill to the north-west) in the relief format the terrain plugin reads: // Command plain writes the ground a town grows on: a gentle plain, 4 × 4 km, lower along a river // that crosses it from west to east, with a low hill in the north-west. relieve.json says the // grid's size and place in kilometres; relieve.f32 holds a height in metres per cell. package main import ( "encoding/binary" "encoding/json" "log" "math" "os" ) func main() { const ( columns, rows = 200, 200 // cells cell = 0.02 // kilometres a side: 20 m west, north = -2.0, 2.0 ) heights := make([]float32, 0, columns*rows) for row := range rows { for column := range columns { east := west + (float64(column)+0.5)*cell northing := north - (float64(row)+0.5)*cell heights = append(heights, float32(height(east, northing))) } } header, _ := json.Marshal(map[string]any{"columns": columns, "rows": rows, "cell": cell, "west": west, "north": north, "units": "km"}) if err := os.WriteFile("relieve.json", header, 0o644); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } file, err := os.Create("relieve.f32") if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } defer file.Close() if err := binary.Write(file, binary.LittleEndian, heights); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } } // height rises gently to the north, dips along the river and swells into a hill to the north-west. func height(east, north float64) float64 { river := 0.1 * math.Sin(east*2) // the river's line, a little winding valley := -6 * math.Exp(-math.Pow((north-river)/0.25, 2)) hill := 35 * math.Exp(-(math.Pow(east+1.2, 2)+math.Pow(north-1.2, 2))/0.4) return 40 + 4*north + valley + hill } go run ./plain Looking at the town A run without a window writes the town as GeoJSON: buildings with their height, parcels, streets, squares, walls, gates and the river. Go Scene Builder turns that into a 3D scene with a style . town.yaml : units: m chunk: 0.5 environment: {sun: [220, 35]} terrain: {color: "#8fa35a"} relations: facing: {when: {kind: street}, reach: 15} rules: - when: {kind: parcel} shape: {role: ground, lift: 0.1} color: "#7f9a4e" - when: {kind: street} shape: {role: ground, width: "width * 1000", lift: 0.3} color: "#d8cdb4" - when: {kind: square} shape: {role: ground, lift: 0.35} color: "#c9bfa8" material: {pattern: cobbles, scale: 0.4} - when: {kind: river} shape: {role: water, width: "width * 1000"} - when: {kind: bridge} shape: {role: line, follow: level, thickness: "width * 1000", height: 0.5} color: "#9c9486" - when: {kind: building} shape: {role: volume, height: "height * 1000"} walls: {color: ["#e9dfc9", "#efe4cf", "#e2d2b4", "#f1ead9"]} roof: {recipe: gable, pitch: 38, ridge: along_street, eaves: 0.3, color: ["#a4553a", "#9a4b33", "#b0613f"]} facade: {door: {color: "#5b3a26"}, windows: {shutters: ["#2f5d50", "#7a3b2e"]}} - when: {kind: wall} shape: {role: line, height: "height * 1000", thickness: 2.5} color: "#a59c8c" material: {pattern: masonry, scale: 0.6} battlements: {height: 1, width: 1, gap: 1} openings: {where: {kind: street, class: road}, width: 8} decorate: [{recipe: gate_towers, size: 6, height: 12}] - when: {kind: old_wall} shape: {role: line, height: 4, thickness: 2} color: "#9a9182" and look/main.go (from the terrain quest ), which tells the builder the snapshot's map is in kilometres with z to the south: // Command look turns a snapshot's entities into a map go-scene-builder reads: the snapshot writes // [x, z] in kilometres, with z to the south, and the builder needs to be told so. // // go run ./look "results/island 100.geojson" map.geojson package main import ( "encoding/json" "log" "os" ) func main() { content, err := os.ReadFile(os.Args[1]) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } var collection map[string]any if err := json.Unmarshal(content, &collection); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } properties, _ := collection["properties"].(map[string]any) if properties == nil { properties = map[string]any{} } properties["units"], properties["axes"] = "km", "east-south" collection["properties"] = properties out, _ := json.Marshal(collection) if err := os.WriteFile(os.Args[2], out, 0o644); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } } After every run, for year 100: go run ./look "results/town 100.geojson" map.geojson go run ../go-scene-builder/cmd/build-scene -map map.geojson -relief "results/town 100 elevation.json" -style town.yaml -out town.glb go run ../go-renderer/cmd/visor town.glb The pictures were taken with -zoom 0.25 -look-at 0,0 (and closer where it says). Level 1 · The Founder Mission Pieces Time A village where two roads meet city , the inputs, nucleus , population , expand 10 min The idea A town needs somewhere to be and a reason to be there . The plugin reads the first from a map of inputs: the window it may grow in, the roads that already cross it, the river . The second is a population curve : how many people live there each year. Every year the town finds room for them, plot by plot, where they would most want to live: near the centre, on a street. The city rule sets the town up and holds it; the other rules find it by its instance name . Build it inputs.geojson , in world kilometres [x, z] : {"type": "FeatureCollection", "features": [ {"type": "Feature", "properties": {"role": "window"}, "geometry": {"type": "Polygon", "coordinates": [[[-1.5, -1.5], [1.5, -1.5], [1.5, 1.5], [-1.5, 1.5], [-1.5, -1.5]]]}}, {"type": "Feature", "properties": {"role": "river", "width": 0.03}, "geometry": {"type": "LineString", "coordinates": [[-2, 0.07], [-1, -0.09], [0, 0], [1, 0.09], [2, -0.07]]}}, {"type": "Feature", "properties": {"role": "road"}, "geometry": {"type": "LineString", "coordinates": [[-2, -0.4], [-0.6, -0.25], [0, -0.15], [0.7, -0.3], [2, -0.2]]}}, {"type": "Feature", "properties": {"role": "road"}, "geometry": {"type": "LineString", "coordinates": [[0.1, -2], [0.05, -0.6], [0, -0.15], [0.05, 0.4], [0.3, 2]]}} ]} rules.yaml : the terrain plugin puts the plain in the world, and the urban plugin grows on it: plugins: - {name: terrain, command: [go, run, .], directory: ../go-simulator-terrain} - {name: urban, command: [go, run, .], directory: ../go-simulator-urban} stages: - name: town clock: {unit: year, from: -1, to: 10, step: 1} snapshots: [10] rules: - rule: relief with: {path: relieve.json, origin: [0, 0]} - rule: city name: market_town with: features: inputs.geojson seed: 7 nucleus: [0, -0.15] centres: [{at: [0, -0.15], weight: 1}] population: {model: logistic, from_year: 0, from: 300, to_year: 100, to: 6000, ceiling: 7000} max_floors: [{before: 50, floors: 2}, {floors: 3}] - {rule: expand, with: {city: market_town}} - {rule: indicators, with: {city: market_town, years: [10]}} logistic growth starts slowly, speeds up and levels off under a ceiling . go run ../go-simulator/cmd/simulate -rules rules.yaml -output results/ Checkpoint At year 10, a round little square where the roads meet, and houses along the roads near it, their doors on the street. Level 1: houses along four roads round a small square, the river to the south Achievement unlocked: Founder Learn more: Writing a scenario · The model Level 2 · The Builder Mission Pieces Time A century of growth densify , the clock, indicators 6 min The idea A town grows two ways: outwards , new houses on new plots ( expand ), and inwards , houses rebuilt taller and closer as plots fill ( densify ), like a bookshelf that first gets new shelves, then books squeezed in. max_floors says how tall houses may be in each period. Build it Run the whole century, with both rules: clock: {unit: year, from: -1, to: 100, step: 1} snapshots: [10, 50, 100] rules: - … relief and city as before … - {rule: densify, with: {city: market_town}} - {rule: expand, with: {city: market_town}} - {rule: indicators, with: {city: market_town, years: [10, 50, 100]}} Checkpoint By year 50 the town has stretched along all four roads, a street village , one house deep. In results/events.jsonl , the indicators of year 100 count 6,000 inhabitants on about 42 hectares. Level 2: a long cross of houses along the four roads Achievement unlocked: Builder Level 3 · The Planner Mission Pieces Time Streets of its own, behind the frontages open_streets_below , pruning, splitting 6 min The idea When the road frontages are taken, a town either keeps stretching along them, or opens new streets behind them, like a tree growing branches. open_streets_below says when: a town opens a street before building on frontages less wanted than this (0.3 makes street villages, 0.5–0.7 compact towns). Streets that stay empty are pruned; blocks that grow too large are split. Build it In the city's with : open_streets_below: 0.6 . And two rules that tidy the street network every five years: - {rule: prune_empty_streets, with: {city: market_town}, every: 5} - {rule: split_large_blocks, with: {city: market_town}, every: 5} Checkpoint New lanes branch off the roads, with blocks of houses between them: a town, not a cross. Level 3: lanes branching off the roads, blocks of houses between them Achievement unlocked: Planner Level 4 · The Bridge master Mission Pieces Time A town that lives by its river, with squares river , squares , space_syntax 8 min The idea A river is a street of water : plots facing it are wanted, quays line it, bridges cross it where people need to. And where many paths cross, people stop: a square opens. To know where paths cross most, the town measures space syntax : how often each street lies on the shortest way between two places. Build it In the city's with : river: {reach: 0.25} squares: {per_inhabitants: 1500} and two rules: - {rule: space_syntax, with: {city: market_town, samples: 200}, every: 5} - {rule: squares, with: {city: market_town}, every: 5} Checkpoint Close up ( -zoom 0.12 -look-at 0,0.05 ): rows of houses along both banks where the road crosses, and a square by the water. The snapshot now counts two squares. Level 4: houses along both banks of the river, a square by the water Achievement unlocked: Bridge master Level 5 · The Mason Mission Pieces Time A wall, gates, and a wall outgrown first_wall , the walls rule 6 min The idea A town walls itself when it has something to protect : here, once 2,500 people live in it. The wall goes round the built town, with gates where roads leave. When the town spills past it, a new, wider wall is built, and the old one stays as old_wall , like rings in a tree trunk . Build it In the city's with : first_wall: {population: 2500} , and the rule, before the tidying ones: - {rule: walls, with: {city: market_town}} The style already draws wall with battlements and towers at the gates, and old_wall lower. Checkpoint A wide wall round the town with towers where the roads go through, and the line of the first, smaller wall inside it. The snapshot counts wall , old_wall and four gate s. Level 5: a town inside a wide wall, the old wall's line inside Achievement unlocked: Mason Final challenge · Mayor Give the town a second centre north of the river, which starts to draw people in year 40 and takes thirty years to grow; and check the century: about six thousand people at the end (±10 %), and a wall. Hint: centres takes several, each with a weight , grows_from and grows_for . Objectives go in the stage. Careful with commas in names: in {…} , a comma ends the value. Try it on your own first, then compare with the solution. The final challenge: the walled town with a second quarter north of the river Rare achievement unlocked: Mayor Well done All six achievements: Founder, Builder, Planner, Bridge master, Mason and Mayor You founded a town, let it grow for a century by rules of where people want to live, and checked it came out as planned. Ideas to keep going Idea Difficulty Hint Taller in the core ⭐ density and rare_floors ( scenario ) Curvier streets ⭐ organic: {wander_degrees: 20} Watch it grow live ⭐⭐ go-simulator/cmd/simulator with a scene_style (Go Simulator's rules files ) The town on an island of your own ⭐⭐⭐ The terrain and flora quests, with tree_nodes to clear the forest Troubleshooting You see Why, and what to do city: at least one growth centre is needed Add centres: [{at: [x, z], weight: 1}] pkg-config: geos not found Install GEOS: libgeos-dev or geos An objective's name is cut short A comma inside {…} ends the value: write the number in words, or quote the name The town does not grow The population curve starts after the clock, or the window is all obstacles The town is mirrored in the viewer The map was not run through look ← All the documentation

what-it-writes.title: 📤 Outputs
what-it-writes.text: 📤 Outputs Entities The city appears as entities with ground shapes, one batch per kind, so thousands of houses stay cheap to draw. Heights are in world units, exaggerated by height_scale . Properties travel with them, so snapshots can be measured or drawn by other tools. Kind Shape Properties street line with a width class : road (reaches the city from outside), main (most chosen, space syntax), ring (where an old wall stood), street , alley , quay ; from_node , to_node parcel flat outline use , coverage , floors , year , front , depth , street , square_metres building volume (floors × 3.2 m + 2 m) use , floors , parcel wall line with a height year , current , height_m gate a point (its transform), no shape year (of its wall), wall (index of the wall); only the standing wall's gates, where roads and main streets cross it old_wall flat line year square flat outline — bridge line — river line with its width width Uses: housing , shop , workshop , extensive (gardens and convents in the belts where old walls stood) and demolished (taken by a new street, square or wall). The indicators event In the years the indicators rule lists, an indicators event with the measures to compare with historic town centres: Key Measure year , inhabitants , parcels , street_pieces , walls counts settled_hectares ground of the parcels plus 40 % for streets and squares inhabitants_per_hectare density expected_hectares_cesaretti what a European city of this population covered around 1300 (Cesaretti et al. 2016) crossings_per_hectare , mean_street_piece_metres , edges_per_node , share_of_degree_three , share_of_dead_ends street network (Crucitti et al. 2006; Barthelemy and Flammini 2008) mean_block_metres blocks (Siksna 1997) mean_front_metres , mean_depth_metres plots (Conzen 1960) coverage_gsi , floor_area_ratio_far built coverage and floor area ratio Objectives in a rules file can read any of them, for example {event: indicators, value: inhabitants, near: 6000, tolerance: 0.05} .

writing-a-scenario.title: 🗺️ The city's scenario
writing-a-scenario.text: 🗺️ The city's scenario The scenario is the with: of the city rule, or files it includes ( with: {include: [derived.yaml, town.yaml]} ). Coordinates are world coordinates on the ground plane (x, z) in kilometres; relative paths start at the rules file's folder. Keys the plugin does not know are ignored, so a scenario can carry notes for people. - rule: city name: my_town with: features: inputs.geojson nucleus: [0, 0] population: {model: logistic, from_year: 0, from: 300, to_year: 100, to: 6000, ceiling: 8000} centres: [{at: [0, 0], weight: 1}, {at: [0.3, 0.8], weight: 0.9, grows_from: 30, grows_for: 40}] grid: [{from_year: 40, angle_degrees: 20, area: [[x, z], …], block: 0.08}] open_streets_below: 0.3 max_floors: [{before: 40, floors: 2}, {before: 80, floors: 3}, {floors: 4}] rare_floors: {floors: 3, share: 0.05} building_depth: [1, 1.5] first_wall: {year: 60, population: 3000} wall_heights: [[60, 4], [70, 4], [100, 25]] new_wall_when_outside: 0.3 square_metres_per_person: 30 seed: 7 height_scale: 1 Keys Key Default Meaning relief the world's elevation {path, minimum_x, minimum_z, cell_size} : a .npy of heights in metres, rows from the smallest z, placed by its first cell centre features — GeoJSON inputs (see below) nucleus — [x, z] of the first village's square population required {model: logistic, from_year, from, to_year, to, ceiling} ; the ceiling must be above to centres required [{at: [x, z], weight, grows_from, grows_for}] : points that pull the city; a centre can start in a year and grow over some years grid none [{from_year, angle_degrees, area, block}] : zones laid out on a lattice of block km (0.08) open_streets_below 0.3 0.3: street villages along the roads; 0.5–0.7: compact towns with back streets max_floors [{floors: 3}] [{before: year, floors}, …, {floors}] : the most floors in each period rare_floors none {floors, share} : at most this share of the plots may reach these floors, the most wanted ones; plots that already stand that high keep their place building_depth coverage 0.4 → 0.7 [from, to] : houses as deep as from…to times their front first_wall population 3000 {year, population} : the first wall goes up at the population or, at the latest, in the year wall_rise 11 m from the start {from, height, years} : metres the year it goes up, then evenly up to height wall_heights none [[year, metres], …] : the standing wall's height by calendar year; wins over wall_rise new_wall_when_outside 0.3 share of the floor space outside the wall that raises a new one square_metres_per_person 30 floor space a person needs seed 1 the same seed grows the same city height_scale 1 how much buildings are exaggerated in 3D clear_nodes none scene nodes cleared under the clear features at the start tree_nodes none scene nodes of trees, cleared there too and under every new plot colours grey sRGB "#rrggbb" by kind, use or "garden" , for viewing without a scene style organic Curvier organic streets. Key Default Meaning segment 0.055 mean length of a street piece (km) wander_degrees 12 spread of the turn at every piece field_snapping 1 chance a street bends to the tensor field when close to it continuation 1 how much more likely a street goes on from its end than branches closing 1.5 how far ahead (× the piece) a street looks to close a block infill 0 extra want of frontages among built plots, so streets fill before new ones open density From the core to the outskirts. Key Default Meaning core_front_perches , outer_front_perches [1, 1.5], [3, 5] plot fronts, in perches (5.03 m) core_depth , outer_depth [0.025, 0.04], [0.035, 0.05] plot depths (km) core_house_depth , outer_house_depth 2, 1 deepest house, × the front outer_floors 1 most floors in the outskirts radius_factor 0.6 the core's radius, × the growth radius back_buildings_from 0 (never) density from which full plots build at the back, round a yard districts none [{name, area, density}] : areas with their own density squares Irregular squares at busy crossings, gates and bridgeheads: per_inhabitants (2500), spacing (0.2 km), size ([0.012, 0.03] km of reach from the crossing), at_gates (true: a square just inside every gate of the standing wall), at_bridges (true: a square at both ends of every bridge). river How rivers shape the town: reach (0.25 km), alignment (1, weight of the banks in street directions), frontage_bonus (1), quays (true), longest_bridge (1.6 × the river's width), bridge_chance (0.6), bridge_spacing (0.15 km), workshops_by_water (0.3), from_world (false: also take the world's river entities, as the terrain's erosion rule publishes them), narrowest (0 km: world rivers narrower than this are left out). Input features features is a GeoJSON collection; every feature has a role : Role Geometry Meaning window polygon where the city may grow (required) road line roads that already exist; the city grows along them river line, with width (km) a river that crosses the town (see the model) rivers polygon other water, an obstacle obstacles polygon where nothing is built wall_support polygon rock the wall ties to instead of crossing it wall_outline polygon the shape of the wall, when it is given; then it is the only wall clear polygon where the drawn scene is cleared at the start
